record.paper_title: Twenty Open Questions in Supersymmetric Particle Physics
record.original_question: Why should supersymmetric particle physics be embedded in string theory: can a theory whose fundamental objects are one-dimensional strings simultaneously provide quantized gravity through a massless spin-two excitation, improve ultraviolet finiteness relative to point-particle field theory, require gauge symmetry and gauge coupling unification, and explain why supersymmetry should appear at high energies?

evidence.quote: The fundamental tenet underlying string theory is that all of the known elementary particles and gauge bosons can be realized as the different excitation modes of a single fundamental closed string of size ∼ 10−33 cm.

First, one finds that among the excitations of such a string there exists a spin-two massless excitation that is naturally identified as the graviton. Thus string theory is a theory of quantized gravity.
For the purposes of this review, it turns out that the most intriguing aspect of string theory may be that it seems to predict supersymmetry.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a candidate theory of fundamental physics whose elementary objects are one-dimensional extended strings of characteristic length on the order of 10^{-33} cm, whose distinct vibrational/excitation modes are postulated to give rise to all known elementary particles and gauge bosons. Provide a rigorous account that establishes the following four properties of such a string-based framework, and explain in what precise sense each property follows from the one-dimensional nature of the fundamental objects:

1. (Quantized gravity.) Show that the spectrum of excitations of a closed string necessarily contains a massless spin-two state, and explain why this state can be consistently identified with the graviton of a quantum theory of gravity.

2. (Ultraviolet behavior.) Demonstrate that perturbative scattering amplitudes built from string worldsheets exhibit improved ultraviolet behavior compared with the corresponding amplitudes in point-particle quantum field theory, and characterize the mechanism (e.g. modular invariance, soft high-energy behavior) responsible for this improvement.

3. (Gauge symmetry and unification.) Show that consistency of the string theory (anomaly cancellation, modular invariance, tadpole cancellation, etc.) forces the appearance of non-abelian gauge symmetries, and analyze whether and how the gauge couplings of these symmetries are predicted to unify at a high scale.

4. (Necessity of supersymmetry.) Establish under what consistency conditions a string theory containing spacetime fermions must be spacetime supersymmetric, and explain the sense in which supersymmetry is therefore predicted to be present at sufficiently high energies, motivating its relevance for particle physics below the string scale.

The problem is to give a coherent and mathematically precise justification — within a single string-theoretic framework — of all four features simultaneously, identifying the minimal assumptions required and the logical implications among them.
artifact.status_search_result: This is a foundational motivational/conceptual question about why string theory is a natural setting for supersymmetric particle physics. While many of its individual components (massless spin-2 in closed string spectra, improved UV behavior, gauge symmetries from heterotic/Type I constructions, spacetime supersymmetry from worldsheet supersymmetry and GSO projection) are well-established results in string theory, the overarching question of whether string theory is the correct embedding for supersymmetric particle physics — and whether it leads to testable predictions such as gauge coupling unification and low-energy supersymmetry — remains open as of recent reviews.
